# Freshman Congressman Trades Apartment for Office Cot Amid Economic Concerns

**WASHINGTON** — For first-term Rep. Daniel Reyes, home isn't a Capitol Hill apartment or a rented townhouse. It's a folding cot tucked behind his office desk, just steps from the House floor.

The 38-year-old congressman, who took office in January, says he made the decision to sleep in his congressional office to avoid the steep cost of maintaining a second residence in one of the nation's most expensive housing markets.

"I've got a mortgage back home and a family to support," Reyes said in an interview. "Paying $3,000 a month for a place I'd barely see didn't make sense to me — especially when so many families in my district are tightening their belts."

## A Growing Trend

Reyes is not alone. Dozens of lawmakers from both parties have reportedly opted to bunk in their offices over the years, a practice that has drawn both praise and criticism. Supporters call it fiscally responsible; critics argue it raises ethical questions about using taxpayer-funded facilities as personal living quarters.

Reyes keeps his arrangement simple. A gym bag holds his clothes, and he showers at the House members' gym facility. His mornings begin early, he said, folding up the cot before staff arrive.

"It's not glamorous," he acknowledged with a laugh. "But it keeps me focused on why I'm here."

## Mixed Reactions

Government watchdog groups have long questioned whether office-sleeping should be permitted. Some argue lawmakers receive a salary — currently $174,000 annually — sufficient to afford housing.

"There's a legitimate debate about whether congressional offices should double as bedrooms," said one ethics analyst. "It blurs the line between public resources and private benefit."

But Reyes' constituents seem largely supportive. At a recent town hall, several attendees applauded when the subject came up.

"He's living like the rest of us are living," said Maria Colton, a small-business owner from Reyes' district. "That means something."

## Staying Grounded

For his part, Reyes says the arrangement helps him stay connected to the economic pressures facing working families back home.

"When I'm voting on a budget, I want to feel the same weight my constituents feel," he said. "This keeps me honest."

Whether the practice remains sustainable through a full term, Reyes isn't sure. But for now, he says, the cot stays.

"Ask me again in two years," he said, smiling. "But I think I'll be just fine."

---

**WASHINGTON** — For most members of Congress, arriving in the nation's capital means signing a lease on a Washington apartment or townhome. For Rep. Jason Chaffetz, R-Utah, it means unrolling a cot next to his office desk and calling it a night.

The Utah congressman has forgone renting a home in the Washington area, instead choosing to sleep on a folding cot in his congressional office—a decision he says reflects both his fiscal principles and his connection to the constituents back home.

"I get the best night's sleep I can possibly get right here in the office," Chaffetz told reporters, gesturing toward the modest cot tucked away during working hours. "I come here to work, not to set up a second life in Washington."

## A Matter of Principle—and Practicality

Chaffetz frames the arrangement as consistent with his message of frugality and limited government. Washington rents run steep, and the congressman says he'd rather not maintain two households while separated from his family, who remain in Utah.

"My family is in Utah. That's my home," he said. "When I'm here, I'm working. When Congress isn't in session, I want to be back with my wife and kids—not paying rent on an empty apartment in D.C."

The routine has its rhythms. Chaffetz showers in the House gym facilities available to members, keeps his workday clothes in the office, and folds away his bedding each morning before staff and visitors arrive.

## Not Entirely Alone

Chaffetz isn't the only lawmaker to embrace the office-as-bedroom approach. Dozens of members from both parties reportedly bunk down in their offices, forming an informal fraternity of cot-dwellers who swap tips on the best showering schedules and how to catch some rest amid late-night votes.

Critics have occasionally questioned the practice, raising concerns about members effectively living in taxpayer-funded federal buildings. Some have suggested the sleeping arrangements amount to an untaxed housing benefit. Chaffetz waves off such objections, insisting he's saving money rather than exploiting a perk.

## Staying Grounded

Supporters see the choice as a symbol of a lawmaker determined to avoid "going Washington."

"He's not here to get comfortable inside the Beltway," said one admirer from his district. "He's here to do a job and go home."

For Chaffetz, the cot serves as a nightly reminder of why he came to Washington in the first place.

"Every time I lie down on that cot, I remember I'm a guest in this town," he said. "Utah is home. This is just where the work gets done."

As the lights dim in the Longworth building each evening, a Utah congressman settles onto his cot—proof that in Washington, at least one representative is quite literally sleeping on the job.

---

# In an Era of Belt-Tightening, One Lawmaker Takes Frugality to the Extreme

*As the recession deepens, Rep. Daniel Reyes sleeps in his office and bikes to the Capitol. Critics call it a stunt. He calls it solidarity.*

---

WASHINGTON — At 5:45 a.m., while most of Capitol Hill still sleeps, the fluorescent lights flicker on in Room 1204 of the Longworth House Office Building. Behind a folding screen in the corner, Rep. Daniel Reyes rolls up an air mattress and stows it beneath his desk, next to a mini-refrigerator and a well-worn pair of cycling shoes.

For the past eight months, this cramped office has doubled as the congressman's home.

"I couldn't look my constituents in the eye and tell them to tighten their belts while I kept a second apartment on the taxpayer's dime," Reyes said, pouring instant coffee into a chipped mug bearing his district's seal. "If families in my district are choosing between rent and groceries, the least I can do is give up my own comforts."

## A Recession Bites

The nation's economic downturn, now entering its fourteenth month, has hollowed out communities across Reyes's largely working-class district. Unemployment there has climbed past nine percent. Food bank lines stretch around city blocks. Two manufacturing plants that once anchored the local economy have shuttered since spring.

Against that backdrop, Reyes has staged what he describes as a personal austerity campaign. He gave up his rented apartment, returning the housing portion of his allowance. He commutes the four miles from his office to committee hearings by bicycle. He has publicly declined a portion of his congressional salary, redirecting it to local charities, and he eats most meals from a rotating supply of canned goods and produce he buys in bulk.

"People are hurting," he said. "I don't need a chef and a townhouse to do this job."

## Praise, and Plenty of Skeptics

Reyes's approach has earned him a national profile — and no small amount of criticism. Detractors argue that his gestures are political theater that does little to address structural economic problems.

"Look, I respect Dan personally, and I don't doubt he means well," said Rep. Karen Whitfield, who represents the neighboring district. "But sleeping under your desk doesn't create a single job. We need real policy — infrastructure investment, small business relief, extended unemployment benefits. Symbolism is not a substitute for legislation."

Whitfield, seated in her considerably tidier office one floor up, chose her words carefully. "There's a fine line between leadership and performance," she added. "I worry that the cameras following him around distract from the hard, unglamorous work of actually governing us out of this mess."

Reyes bristles at the suggestion that his lifestyle is a publicity stunt.

"Karen and I want the same things," he countered. "But you can't ask people to sacrifice if you're not willing to sacrifice yourself. I'm not saying my air mattress is going to fix the economy. I'm saying it's a matter of credibility."

## The Human Cost of a Symbol

Not everyone in Reyes's orbit is convinced the arrangement is sustainable. Staffers, speaking on condition of anonymity, describe an office culture strained by their boss's around-the-clock presence and a certain performative intensity. Ethics experts have raised questions about whether living in a congressional office runs afoul of chamber rules — a gray area that House administrators have so far declined to formally address.

Reyes waves off such concerns. "Rules are written for people trying to get around them," he said. "I'm trying to do the opposite."

By 7 a.m., he was clipping into his bicycle pedals for the ride to a hearing on unemployment insurance. He plans to keep this up, he says, "for as long as the recession lasts — however long that is."

Whether his frugality reflects genuine conviction or shrewd political calculation may ultimately matter less than what it reveals about a nation on edge, watching its leaders for any sign that they, too, feel the pinch.

"Maybe it's a small thing," Reyes said, adjusting his helmet. "But small things add up. That's what my mother always told me. In a recession, that's about all any of us can hold onto."

*—Additional reporting contributed by the Capitol Hill bureau.*
